title: Maximum Distance Between a Pair of Values
statement:
Both `nums1` and `nums2` are integer arrays sorted in non-increasing order (each element is at most the one before it). An index pair `(i, j)`, with `i` a position of `nums1` and `j` a position of `nums2`, is *valid* when `i <= j` and `nums1[i] <= nums2[j]`; its distance is `j - i`.

Return the largest distance over all valid pairs, or `0` if no pair is valid.
constraints: nums1 and nums2 are both non-increasing
notes:
## Intuition

Checking every pair is O(n · m). The sorted order gives a shortcut. As `i` moves right, `nums1[i]` can only shrink, so the positions in `nums2` that are large enough for it can only reach further. That means neither index ever has to move backwards: two pointers walking in the same direction see every pair that could be the best one.

## Approach

1. Start `i` and `j` at `0` and `best` at `0`.
2. While both indices are in range, compare `nums1[i]` with `nums2[j]`.
3. If `nums1[i] <= nums2[j]`, the pair satisfies the value rule: record `j - i` in `best` (a negative value when `j < i` never wins), then move `j` right to look for a farther match.
4. Otherwise `nums2[j]` is too small for `nums1[i]`, and every later `nums2` value is no bigger, so this `i` is finished: move `i` right to a smaller value.
5. Return `best`.

## Example 1, step by step

`nums1 = [55, 30, 5, 4, 2]`, `nums2 = [100, 20, 10, 10, 5]`.

- `(0, 0)`: `55 <= 100`, `best = 0`, `j = 1`.
- `(0, 1)`: `55 > 20`, `i = 1`. `(1, 1)`: `30 > 20`, `i = 2`.
- `(2, 1)`: `5 <= 20`, distance `-1`, `j = 2`. `(2, 2)`: distance 0, `j = 3`. `(2, 3)`: distance 1, `best = 1`, `j = 4`.
- `(2, 4)`: `5 <= 5`, distance 2, `best = 2`, `j = 5`, and the loop ends.

The answer is `2`.

## Complexity

- Time: O(n + m): each step moves `i` or `j` forward by one.
- Space: O(1).

## Pitfalls

- Only count pairs with `i <= j`; taking `Math.max` with `best` starting at `0` quietly ignores pairs where `j < i`.
- Return `0`, not `-1`, when no pair is valid.
- The arrays are non-increasing, so "large enough" values sit at the front of `nums2`; a binary search for each `i` must look for the last index with `nums2[j] >= nums1[i]`.

## Variables

| Name | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `i` | current index in `nums1` |
| `j` | current index in `nums2` |
| `best` | largest valid distance found so far |

narration.2: i points into nums1, starting at its largest value.
narration.3: j points into nums2, also starting at the front.
narration.4: No valid pair is known yet, so the best distance is 0.
narration.6: Continue while both pointers are still inside their arrays.
narration.7: Does nums2[j] reach at least nums1[i]?
narration.8: Yes: the pair passes the value test, so record its distance; a negative distance never beats best.
narration.9: Try a farther j for the same i.
narration.11: No: no later nums2 value is big enough for nums1[i], so move to the next, smaller nums1 value.
narration.14: Every useful pair was seen; return the largest distance.
